 Rain break, but Bengaluru’s water woes persist
 By Sridhar Vivan Sridhar Vivan / Updated: Oct 16, 2026, 06:00 IST

 Linkedin 
 Email 
 Share 
 Facebook

 Print this article Reduce font size Increase font size Motorists speed past on a rainy Thursday evening in the city Forecast showers offer hope as Bengaluru battles unusual October heat, while falling KRS storage heightens concerns over future supplies 
Bengaluru is set to witness a spell of rain over the next three days, even as the city continues to record above-normal temperatures and concerns grow over drinking water availability following a sharp fall in the water level of the Krishnaraja Sagar reservoir.
The India Meteorological Department has forecast cloudy skies, gusty winds and intermittent thunderstorms in Bengaluru until October 18. Winds may reach speeds of 30–40 kmph, while temperatures are expected to remain between 20°C and 30°C. The forecast has brought some relief after weeks of hot and dry conditions in the city.
 The rain is linked to a low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal, which has created favourable conditions for the northeast monsoon. The northeast monsoon has already entered parts of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, with rain expected in Bengaluru city and rural areas from Thursday. However, the IMD has warned that the northeast monsoon could still end with a deficit of nearly 30% this year.
Meteorologists said the city’s weather has remained unusually warm for October. Bengaluru recorded a maximum temperature of 31.3°C, around 3.3°C above the normal level of 28°C. While rain is expected in parts of the state, several districts continue to experience intense heat, creating a mixed pattern of scorching sunshine and sudden showers. Bengaluru Urban, Bengaluru Rural, Bengaluru South and Tumakuru have been placed under a yellow alert for October 16 because of the possibility of heavy rain. Coastal districts, including Uttara Kannada, Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, are also facing high temperatures, with a heatwave warning issued for some areas.
The sharp variation in weather has also raised health concerns. Doctors have advised residents, particularly parents, to ensure that children drink sufficient water and remain hydrated. Dehydration and other heat-related complaints are being reported in parts of the state, while children are considered particularly vulnerable to the effects of prolonged heat.
The rain forecast comes at a crucial time for Bengaluru, which depends significantly on the Cauvery system for its drinking water needs. The KRS reservoir, one of the key reservoirs in the Cauvery basin, recorded a water level of just 100.50 feet on Wednesday evening, against its maximum storage level of 124.80 feet. The decline follows a weak southwest monsoon and reduced inflows into the reservoir. The inflow was recorded at 574 cusecs, against an outflow of 2,658 cusecs, leaving the reservoir with 23.057 TMC of water. The water level had last witnessed such a sharp fall in 2016, when it dropped to 81.40 feet. The reservoir will also have to support water releases to Tamil Nadu, irrigation requirements and the needs of people and livestock through rivers and canals until the next monsoon. With storage continuing to fall, farmers and officials are watching the weather closely.
Experts said that although the expected rain could provide temporary relief and improve inflows, officials and residents may need more than a few showers to ease the city’s longer-term drinking water concerns. The performance of the northeast monsoon over the coming weeks will therefore be crucial for Bengaluru’s water security.
